gallery.filename: Oxfam East Africa - New camp stands idle and closed as Somali refugees pour into Kenya.jpg
gallery.title: File:Oxfam East Africa - New camp stands idle and closed as Somali refugees pour into Kenya.jpg
gallery.credit: New camp stands idle and closed as Somali refugees pour into Kenya
gallery.source: Oxfam East Africa - New camp stands idle and closed as Somali refugees pour into Kenya
gallery.description:
The new Ifo II camp was built to try and ease the severe overcrowding in Dadaab, where camps designed for 90,000 people now shelter over 380,000. Yet despite the influx of new arrivals, Ifo II remains empty as the Government of Kenya has refused to allow people to move in. Water systems, latrines and healthcare facilities are ready to use but are standing idle. Another planned extension known as Ifo III has also stalled. Meanwhile 60,000 new refugees are sheltering a few kilometres away and desperately need services such as these. 

More: oxf.am/4xK

gallery.description: Children have walked for weeks across the desert to get to Dadaab, and many perish on the way. Others have died shortly after arrival. On the edge of the camp, a young girl stands amid the freshly made graves of 70 children, many of whom died of malnutrition. Photo: Andy Hall/Oxfam.

gallery.title: File:Oxfam East Africa - New arrivals wait to get processed.jpg
gallery.credit: New arrivals wait to get processed
gallery.source: Oxfam East Africa - New arrivals wait to get processed
gallery.description: Nearly 60,000 people arrived in Dadaab last month, fleeing the food crisis in Somalia. The majority are women and children, many of whom have braved a difficult and dangerous journey across the desert to get here. These new arrivals wait to be registered - many of them face a wait of more than six weeks for registration due to delays and the massive influx. In the meantime they receive food rations that will last 21 days at most. Photo: Andy Hall/Oxfam

gallery.filename: Oxfam East Africa - Oxfam workers distribute aid in Dadaab camp.jpg
gallery.title: File:Oxfam East Africa - Oxfam workers distribute aid in Dadaab camp.jpg
gallery.description: Oxfam health workers in Dadaab prepare to distribute 7,000 jerry cans and bars of soap to newly arrived refugees who have walked for many days across the desert from Somalia. The Dadaab camps are severely overcrowded and clean water is scarce. Without sanitised jerry cans to store the water, it can quickly become contaminated and risk spreading disease. The soap also helps to improve sanitation in the camp and reduces the risk of potentially fatal illnesses such as diarrhoea, especially among children

gallery.filename: Oxfam East Africa - Hundreds of families are arriving in Dadaab camp every day 01.jpg
gallery.title: File:Oxfam East Africa - Hundreds of families are arriving in Dadaab camp every day 01.jpg
gallery.description:
Madina Farah Yusuf arrived in Dadaab a week ago after walking for 10 days with her seven children. On the way she came across four other young children who had lost their parents. She took them in and brought them all to Dadaab, where they are now taking shelter under a tree:
“We left Somalia in fear our lives. There was so much hunger and war. Bandits robbed us of our food and clothes on the way. I found these four young children as we came. They were on their own as their mother had died of starvation. We brought everyone here (Dadaab) as we thought we could get help. But we stay under this tree. .
“It gets very cold at night, and the children cry. We only have one blanket. It is also unprotected out in the open. I worry that hyenas will attack the children. .

“We drank some tea this morning, but we have very little food. The rations are not enough for everyone to eat everyday. We have some water (there is now an Oxfam pump a few hundred metres away) but we need shelter and toilets."

gallery.title: File:Living conditions in Dadaab (7554218978).jpg
gallery.description:
For the tens of thousands of people who arrived in the camp last year, many remain living in basic shelters like this. They are exposed to the harsh climate, and much of the plastic sheeting that was distributed last year has now worn out. They are also left vulnerable to the insecurity in the camp. At the moment 30,000 new shelters are needed, yet funding is only available for 4,000. 

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:An aid warehouse (7554223204).jpg
gallery.description:
Aid supplies at a warehouse in Dadaab. Funding shortfalls mean that many essential services such as water, healthcare, education and sanitation may have to be cut in the coming months.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:Building latrines to improve sanitation (7554222218).jpg
gallery.description:
Men are building latrine slabs which will become family toilets. The men are refugees who are paid by Oxfam for their labour. Jobs are scarce in Dadaab and people struggle to make a living, so this provides them with a temporary income to feed their families.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.filename: A recently arrived family in Dadaab (7554224360).jpg
gallery.title: File:A recently arrived family in Dadaab (7554224360).jpg
gallery.description:
Last year 160,000 people arrived in Dadaab, increasing the size of the already overcrowded camp by a third. Some families are still fleeing the ongoing conflict in Somalia. Fatuma Sankos arrived in Dadaab two months ago with her two small sons - Abass Hassan and Mohamed Hassan. She lives in a tiny shelter made from sticks, cardboard and plastic bags. She has not yet been formally registered in the camp so is not able to get food rations and depends on other refugees for food, and aid agencies for water. 

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:Collecting water (7554217754).jpg
gallery.description:
Oxfam is providing clean water to thousands of families who have arrived in the past year. From September 2012, funding for new water and sanitation systems is set to run out.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:An Oxfam hygiene kit (7550591314).jpg
gallery.description:
Disease can spread quickly in a place like Dadaab, where many people are crowded together in basic conditions. As part of efforts to reduce this threat, Oxfam distributes hygiene kits including soap, buckets and jerry cans for storing water safely.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:Mohamed, the school teacher (7550595424).jpg
gallery.description:
Mohamed Hassan Dirige is a secondary school teacher in Dadaab. He arrived here in 1991 at the age of five. When still in Somalia, armed men lined him and his family up, bound their hands together and shot each person leaving them for dead. He survived and made it to Dadaab, where he now earns 8000 Kenyan shillings (about $95) per month from teaching. This must be shared with his entire family, leaving them with less than $0.70 each per day to live on. He still receives food rations and would like nothing more than to return to his home country where he can earn a better wage.
Many children in Dadaab are out of school. Often classes have over 100 pupils and only one-in-five teachers have formal training.    

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:Hassan the bookseller (7550602404).jpg
gallery.description:
In the more established camps of Dadaab, such as Ifo 1 and Hagadera, small shops have sprung up. Hassan Moham Dahir works at the Iftin Bookshop, where he earns 6000 Kenyan shillings (about $71) per month. Hassan was only one year old when his family left Somalia and he has now lived in Dadaab for 22 years.
Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

.

gallery.title: File:Inside the beauty salon (7550608684).jpg
gallery.description:
Asha Mohamed, 20, is the owner of Cadaalo Beauty Salon. She has had no formal training but has been running the business for one year. Asha arrived in Dadaab with her sister in 2008. Her mother still lives in Somalia but she does not know where.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam

gallery.title: File:Mobile phone shop (7550611126).jpg
gallery.description:
Mohammed Abdille Aden is the manager of E-Talk Wireless, a small shop that opened two months ago. It sells mobile phones and accessories and even has a wireless internet connection. Like much of the world, mobile phones are increasingly common in Dadaab - although many people cannot afford them. They help refugees to stay in touch with family members elsewhere.

Photo: Jo Harrison/Oxfam
